items.question: How do you think about getting ahead of established leaders in AI research?
items.object: Getting ahead of established leaders in AI research
items.answer: I think there was a lucky part: the first thing I did in my PhD was actually build agents based on language models. You need to make a different bet in order to surpass the previous leader, right? I mean, if OpenAI had kept doing reinforcement learning, it might also have found it hard to surpass DeepMind. My advisor was the second author of GPT-1, and at the time he was somewhat skeptical about this. One interesting thing is that traditionally people think it happens like this: a big company first creates something, and then startups can start copying it, right? For example, if I create ChatGPT, others can copy ChatGPT or do something similar. But now it seems the reverse can also hold.

items.question: What attracts you to language and agents as a path to general AI?
items.object: Language and agents as a path to general AI
items.answer: I think it is their generality. Almost anything can be represented in language. What attracted me was an intuition I vaguely had at the time: ultimately, if you wanted to achieve AGI—though nobody was talking about AGI at the time—or if you wanted a very general system, you needed to build an agent. Looking back at AI history, from Newell and Simon in the 1960s, the original idea was to build an agent. People were very ambitious: we wanted to solve vision in one summer, language in another, put those things together, build an agent, and then it would be smarter than humans. Even if you look at Turing's original ideas, people naturally wanted to build a person or an agent. But it was too hard, so AI gradually became very fragmented, and the problems people researched grew smaller and smaller. Some people studied how to solve one small part of vision, or language, or an even narrower part such as translation. It became increasingly specialized and vertical. But after 2015, with the emergence of scaling laws and many research breakthroughs, the broad historical trend has been that we should return from vertical thinking to more general thinking and attempt to build a more general system.

items.question: Why did you come to prefer GPT over BERT for building language agents?
items.object: GPT versus BERT for language agents
items.answer: My biggest lesson in the first year was: use GPT, not BERT. At the time, the hottest model in language was BERT. Its idea was to learn a representation: given a sentence, learn a representation of that sentence in some way, then use the representation for many downstream tasks, such as multiple-choice or other selection-based tasks. At the time, perhaps 95 percent of people were working on BERT, and only 5 percent on GPT. That was because the main NLP tasks then were things like classifying whether a sentence was positive or negative—for instance, “I hate this movie” is a negative sentence. For such simple tasks, BERT was indeed better. But to make an agent, you need more than selection ability; you need the ability to freely generate new actions. Of course, in Go or video games, your choices are limited. In Super Mario Bros., perhaps they are just up, down, left, and right. But in a language-based game, actions are free-form: I can kill this monster with this sword, go to the third room, or open the first room's door with my golden key. BERT could never do that. After discovering this, I never used BERT again.

items.question: What do you look for in a research task or environment for language agents?
items.object: Research tasks and environments for language agents
items.answer: My second lesson was that tasks or environments are very important. With a very poor task, you can never learn something very good. At the time, many people worked on tasks that now seem simple, such as whether a sentence is positive or negative, or whether sentence A entails sentence B. They seemed difficult then, but now look very simple. First, you need a sufficiently challenging task—one that can lead to fundamentally new methods. At the time, if you wanted to make agents or language agents, you had little choice but text games such as Zork. Zork is a classic text game: in a text-based world, like an interactive script, you can move down or up, visit rooms, and do all kinds of things. But the environment had many shortcomings. What you could accomplish was limited to that environment; it was not large enough. And if you learned it with RL, as with traditional video games, you could beat the game but gain no transfer to any other task. You can become very good at Go, but it has no value for anything else in the world. I felt we might need a better environment.

items.question: How do you see the common thread running through your language-agent research, from WebShop to ReAct?
items.object: The research approach connecting WebShop and ReAct
items.answer: From my perspective, it was a very natural process. Once I realized there was a problem with the environment, my first relatively important work was WebShop. I felt we first needed to solve the environment problem, because without a good task or environment, it is meaningless no matter how high I push the score in a game. In 2015 there was already a very good work called World of Bits. Its idea was that we should use computers or the internet as an environment—more exciting than games. But because of various technical limitations, it was not done especially well. In 2021, my advisor and I discussed whether it was a natural time to revisit this. Of course, I felt the technology was still not mature; most people were still studying whether A entails B, translation, or answering questions from articles. Building internet agents was not entirely technically mature, but perhaps precisely because it was not mature, it was a good time to start. By 2022, we made the WebShop environment. In 2022, GPT-3 and later Chain of Thought created opportunities for new methods, and we made ReAct. I still think ReAct may be my favorite work. After that, it was natural to do more methods and tasks along those two lines. My research has been, on the one hand, how to create valuable tasks and environments grounded more in the real world; and on the other, how to create simple, general methods.

items.question: How do you assess whether ReAct marked a paradigm shift?
items.object: ReAct and the value of prompting as research
items.answer: I think we may need to look back five or ten years later. It is often hard to tell when something has just been proposed. At the time, academia was still not very able to accept using prompting as research. Traditionally, you needed to propose something fancy—mathematical formulas, train a model, prove that you had done theory or engineering. But if you merely used a model, it felt too soft. Yet in some sense, the most valuable thing then was to study how to use models. If you wanted to train models, you were already years behind OpenAI or those companies, and they might have discovered what you were doing years earlier. If you wanted to do something different, studying how to use models was probably more valuable.

items.object: Language-model agents and a preference for simple, general research methods
items.answer: I think luck played a part: the first thing I did in my PhD was agents based on language models. The consensus was to do question answering, translation, or tasks already accepted by the community. I have always had this non-consensus inclination: I wanted to make agents. Another point is that I have always wanted to make things that are simple and general. I did not want to make something complex that only works in one domain. For example, many people working on question answering designed very complex architectures and did many things around retrieval—how to put context into the model—but in the end it might only work for one task. I have always wanted simple, general things. Traditionally, that was difficult to accept because people were accustomed to continuously subdividing AI problems and developing many specialized methods. Before around 2020, people perhaps did not want to make something very simple and general, or did not believe it was possible.

items.question: How do you define an AI agent across different research contexts?
items.object: The definition of an AI agent
items.answer: I think it depends on the context of the discussion. Historically, from an NLP perspective, an agent is contrasted with a system that generates articles or dialogue: it can interact with the outside world, for example by using a calculator, the internet, or tools. From the NLP perspective, an agent can not only generate new text or thoughts, but also interact with the external world. But in the broader AI context, agent is a very old concept: any system that can make its own decisions, interact with its environment, and optimize reward—that is, increase its reward—is an agent. From this perspective, what people mean by agent today is more often a system based on large models such as language models that can make autonomous decisions, rather than traditional agents based purely on rules or RL acquired in a single domain. The word agent has had many forms in different eras. AlphaGo can be called an agent, Waymo can be called an agent, and a robot can be called an agent. The term is very context-dependent.

items.question: What do you see as the essential difference between language agents and traditional AI agents?
items.object: Language agents and reasoning as a basis for generalization
items.answer: I think the essential difference is that it can reason, because reasoning enables generalization. A simple example: a strong motivation for ReAct, after I finished CALM, my first work, was thinking about why I could immediately play a new game while existing systems or AI needed hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, or millions of training steps. I realized it seemed to be because I could think. When I see a completely new environment, I think: the light is off, so there may be danger; based on common sense, there may be monsters; the most important thing now may be to turn on the light; and from earlier context, the light is behind me, so I should first go backward. Without such thinking ability, directly predicting that I should move backward from a complex language input would be difficult. Without reasoning, it cannot be done. The biggest difference is that language models provide a sufficiently strong prior, which lets you reason, and reasoning in turn lets you generalize across environments.

items.question: How do you understand the evolution of AI agents from symbolic AI to agents built on large language models?
items.object: The evolution of AI agents from symbolic AI through deep reinforcement learning to large language models
items.answer: I can share my own understanding, though it may be incomplete or contain errors. I think the earliest AI was what we call good old-fashioned AI, or symbolic AI. The idea was simple: I focus on reasoning, and I encode the rules of how I think so that AI does the same. For example, if the temperature is above 30 degrees, the air conditioner should cool down. AI based on such rules created many of the earliest agents, including early robots, systems for proving mathematical theorems, and many others. But by the 1980s people found it had a bottleneck. No matter how many rules you wrote, it was difficult to cover every possible situation in the world. Symbolic AI was pushed to its extreme through expert systems: find many experts and write down every possible rule, and perhaps then we would have AGI or a very general useful system. But no matter how many rules you wrote, there were still special cases you could not handle, and those rules only worked for that single task. You could write a heart-disease diagnosis system with many rules, but it could not cover every possible case, because people can say anything, and it could not handle lung disease. That led to the first AI winter. Then came neural networks. I think the second wave of agents was deep reinforcement learning, marked by DeepMind's video games and AlphaGo, and OpenAI playing robotic-hand tasks, Dota, and other games. The core was that you had a virtual environment you could play infinitely many times, a reward, and a very general network architecture; then, as a black box, you learned to improve the reward, and it became stronger. This had many successes, most famously AlphaGo. But it had the same problem: in every environment you needed much environment-specific engineering, such as hyperparameter tuning, engineering, and many other things for Dota. The greatest problem was still its inability to generalize. An agent trained for Go could not play another game; what you learned in one environment could not generalize to another. And if all your environments are virtual or infinitely replayable like games, you cannot find good real-world applications. I think the third wave of agents began with large language models. We found they can reason, and based on reasoning, you can operate in new environments: coding, the internet, and all kinds of digital environments. These digital environments are largely language-based and require reasoning. The main difference in this wave has two sides. In method, we use language models and reasoning to build agents that handle all kinds of problems. In environments, agents have evolved from symbolic-AI tasks like theorem proving, through Go and games, to the real-world digital environments of the internet, coding, and computers. There are two lines here. People often see the methods line but overlook the tasks line; I think they complement each other.

items.question: Why do you see code as one of the most important environments for AI agents?

items.question: How do you view pursuing coding-agent research when other researchers do not seem to recognize its importance?
items.object: Pursuing overlooked coding-agent research through InterCode
items.answer: As early as 2022, I felt very strongly that coding agents were clearly the most important thing—so why was nobody doing them? At the time we made a work called InterCode. Everyone else had a task, generated a piece of code, and evaluated it. We asked: why not return the execution result to the model, make it a multi-turn agent task, and turn it into an environment rather than a simple task? items.question: How do you think AI agents will ultimately use code and APIs versus human-facing graphical interfaces?
items.object: Code and API interfaces versus human-facing graphical interfaces for AI agents
items.answer: In a broader sense, I would view APIs as part of code. Any code-based interface is part of the code environment. I think the ultimate outcome will meet in the middle: both sides will be done. And perhaps it is not that difficult. Coding is certainly important, but GUIs and other things are not that hard either; the eventual agent may do everything.

items.question: How do you assess the prospect of a general AI agent that can carry out nearly any task on human computers and phones?
items.object: General AI agents and the bottleneck to creating value
items.answer: I do not think this is well defined yet. I think the hardest problem for people, or humanity, is often not reasoning, but acquiring context or background—I do not know how best to translate that. items.question: What principles guide how you define rewards for reinforcement-learning tasks?
items.object: Reward design for reinforcement-learning tasks
items.answer: Different people have different flavors and preferences. From very early on, I have had this preference: I want to define a reward based on outcomes rather than process, one based on rules or that can be calculated clearly, rather than one based on human preferences, model preferences, or very black-box things. When we did WebShop, the hardest issue was how to define the reward. In fact, I think the hardest part of any RL task is defining the reward. You can always build all kinds of environments—Amazon or Facebook, for example. This is very difficult engineering-wise, but it can always be done. The hardest part is designing a task that is difficult, has real value, has a good reward, and whose reward is not too noisy: a rule-based or white-box reward, not a black-box reward. Later facts proved that this is the key to RL's success today. The most important feature of tasks such as math and coding is, first, that they are outcome-based rather than process-based. Second, they have a clear, rule-based reward rather than a reward based on strange human or model preferences. If the answer is three, it is three: if the final answer is three, it is correct; if it is not three, it is incorrect. Any other design seems to create hacking. If you define reward based on process, you may get hacking. If you optimize human or machine preferences, you may also get hacking. You may produce very elegant code that does not solve the problem. Other tasks I have done have the same flavor, such as SWE-bench, QA, and various other tasks. items.question: How do you think about classifying agent applications by the difficulty of the tasks they perform?
items.object: Classifying agent applications by task difficulty
items.answer: I currently lean toward the view that there will be different kinds of applications and different challenges, and these may be orthogonal. It is hard to say which is harder or easier. Humanity has a similar issue: who is more formidable, Rockefeller or Einstein? It is hard to define. Which is harder: becoming the CEO of a large company or becoming a mathematician? They may simply be different kinds of difficulty and challenge. For agents, there is another point: a task that is easy or hard for a person may not have the same distinction for an agent. For people, being a customer-service representative may be far easier than being a software engineer. It pays less and requires fewer credentials. Yet now I think being a software engineer is easier than being customer service, because software engineering has a better environment, clearer reward, more data, and other advantages. Making customer service very robust or reliable poses a reliability challenge. We can divide human jobs into various categories, but people themselves face many different aspects of challenge, and the relative difficulty of those challenges does not fully carry over to machines or AI.

items.question: How do you distinguish tasks that demand reliability from tasks that demand creativity when thinking about agents?
items.object: Reliability versus creativity as requirements for agent tasks
items.answer: At a very high level, there are different ways to divide tasks. One division is that some tasks emphasize reliability and others creativity. I can try a hundred times; if I do it exceptionally well once, I succeed. These two categories have different challenges.

items.question: How do you think agent evaluation should reflect the different reliability requirements of practical applications?
items.object: Agent evaluation metrics and robustness in practical applications
items.answer: I think we can do many different things in parallel. There is also a very simple way to design the ordering. In coding, there is a traditional metric called pass@K, meaning that if you write the same code K times, what is the probability that you succeed at least once? As K grows, the probability of success increases. Often coding research reports pass@100: for the same task, if I run it 100 times, what is the probability that I succeed at least once? But last year we released research called TopBench. Its idea was that for another type of task, such as customer service, you need the exactly mirror-opposite metric, which we called pass^K—where the hat is the exponent symbol—meaning the probability of succeeding every time across K attempts, or the probability of failing at least once. In a sense, some tasks require optimizing pass@K, while others require optimizing pass^K. But we now tend to value success rate, which is pass@1, or pass@100. For coding, we do not especially value robustness on simple tasks. I think that is because people are still doing benchmarks in AI—doing tasks rather than practical applications. But once you make that mindset shift, it becomes natural: some applications require robustness, so we need to optimize robustness. items.question: Where do you see the greatest opportunity for agent startups as models become more capable?
items.object: Agent startups’ opportunities as model capabilities improve
items.answer: I think what startups should worry about is models having no spillover capability. In that case, you truly cannot do anything. Spillover capability is very good; it basically means you have an opportunity. The largest opportunity for startups is designing different interfaces, or different ways for people to interact with the digital world. ChatGPT and all model companies are making products similar to ChatGPT. ChatGPT's essence is that you interact with the digital world as if interacting with a person: across from your chatbot is something like a person, and you chat with it, assign it tasks, ask it to do deep research, or ask it to write code. Its interaction mode resembles interaction with a person or an assistant. If you can use models' general capabilities but create a different interaction mode, you can create huge opportunities. Cursor essentially creates a new interaction mode. It is not an interaction mode like speaking to a person; it is like a copilot, or another new mode. As I write code, it can suggest things or add things for me, but people do not interact with one another like that. That is where its value lies. Ultimately, model capabilities may produce super apps with interaction modes different from ChatGPT's. In that case, the greatest opportunity for startups is to explore new interaction modes while having spillover capabilities from models. Both are indispensable. If you use the old interface and leverage new models, you can easily be replaced by ChatGPT. If your interaction mode resembles ChatGPT, why would ChatGPT not replace you? If you build a new interaction mode but models do not keep improving and producing new spillover capabilities, that is also difficult. The best opportunity is to create new interaction modes while models continuously improve and empower those modes through new spillover capabilities.

items.question: How do you think having a super app like ChatGPT shapes a company's ability to pursue new interaction modes?
items.object: Super apps and the startup opportunities created by their path dependence
items.answer: I think having a super app is a double-edged sword for a company. Once you already have an interaction mode, you inevitably develop path dependence. In 2020, Google had unlimited resources and money, the transformer, and the best research, but its most natural thought was probably how to use those things to improve its search engine. When you have a super app like ChatGPT, your research naturally centers around that super app and its interaction mode. You will explore new products, but even at a large company—Google or OpenAI—most resources will still revolve around the interaction mode of your super app. I think that is the startup opportunity.

items.question: How do you assess the assistant-style interaction depicted in Her as a future way for people to interact with AI agents?
items.object: Assistant-style and novel interaction modes for AI agents
items.answer: To me, Her is basically still an assistant form, except it uses voice rather than text. I think it is clearly a very valuable form. Humans have interacted with one another for thousands, tens of thousands, even millions of years; it is the most natural form for humanity, so it is clearly the most obvious super app. And ChatGPT holds the dominant position in that niche, or rather this is clearly what model companies set out to build. What is less obvious is whether I can build interaction modes unlike interaction with a person. Cursor is a good example. In some sense, Google is also a good example. At the time it was a new method nobody had seen; it was strange. Yahoo, in some sense, was more like the Yellow Pages—an interaction mode more familiar to people—whereas Google was less familiar. Assistants, Her, or interaction modes like interacting with a person are clearly among the most important modes, but there will certainly still be enough opportunities for new interaction modes to emerge.

items.question: What do you think an AI application company needs to build a successful data flywheel?
items.object: Data flywheels at AI application companies
items.answer: I think most companies have not yet formed a data flywheel, right? Most companies still rely on models getting better, and then use the spillover capabilities from those improved models. If you want to have a data flywheel, first you need to be able to train models yourself, and through interaction you need to have a good reward. I think you need a good reward that lets you separate good data from bad data, right? I think a relatively successful example now may be Midjourney, right? It has a very clear reward: which image people prefer. And this reward is aligned with my application: if I make this reward better, my company becomes more successful, the model becomes better, and everything is aligned. Given that, if I can train models myself, I can build a data flywheel. And what you do also has to be relatively non-core, because if it is very core, I can improve that capability through pre-training or RL or other methods, right? I can generalize, or use other approaches. So at present, I feel that most companies do not seem to have formed a flywheel.

items.question: If you were Cursor’s CEO, how would you decide whether to pursue pre-training?
items.object: Cursor’s decision to train models and pursue pre-training
items.answer: I think I would definitely train models, or try to train models. But whether to do pre-training depends on the situation. I think coding is a very core task: all the major companies now will make their models good at coding, right? So all the pre-training, post-training, RL, and all kinds of things will take that into account. In that case, whether you should do it may first depend on how good these closed-source models are; second, how good the open-source models are; then how large the gap is between them; and how much of that gap you can fill—make up, right? But of course, if you have a lot of money and resources and want to do it, I think that is also reasonable.

items.question: How do you see the agent ecosystem evolving from foundation models and reasoning?
items.object: The evolution of the agent ecosystem
items.answer: I think there are two directions. One is how fundamental research evolves, or how the methods evolve. The other is how applications, or their modes of interaction, evolve. To some extent they are certainly related, but I think different people will need to explore different aspects. For example, Cursor does not innovate in products or fundamental research; it innovates in interaction modes. In fundamental research, what I personally consider important includes memory, intrinsic reward, and multi-agent. How can I enable an agent—this also resembles OpenAI's idea of the innovator and the organization, right? As an innovator, first you need long-term memory. For example, if I study the Fermat theorem for twenty years, I need long-term memory. But long-term memory is not enough. You need an intrinsic reward, because until the moment you prove it, you have no external reward. You have not won an award or done anything for which anyone gives you feedback. You need to give yourself feedback. This is the most important thing for every innovator, whether an artist, scientist, writer, or any creator. On the other hand, as an organization, you need to solve how agents collaborate with one another and how multi-agent systems scale. To some extent, today's agents may be like an ordinary college student acting as a digital intern. That may be the third stage, or what we call AGI: the capability to do what an ordinary student at a first-tier university can do on a computer. But the frontier of human society is not that—although that covers 80% or 90% of people. Who do we admire most? On one hand, people who innovate—Einstein, Gauguin, Van Gogh, Beethoven—people who can create new things. On the other, people who can create new organizations or great organizations, like Elon Musk or Steve Jobs. Naturally, these two things are important.

items.question: Why do you think today's AI models have not created enough economic value despite their strength in reasoning, exams, and games?
items.object: The context gap limiting AI models' economic usefulness
items.answer: I do not know how much I can share, but my belief is what I mentioned in my blog: the utility problem. I think the fundamental reason may be that they lack this context. A tricky aspect of human society is that, of course, we write down many things—we use text, Google Docs, Notion, and record many things—but much context exists only in people's minds. It is maintained in a distributed way. For example, your boss's behavioral habits toward you, or things that are hard to summarize in language: that context exists in people's minds. People can never write all of it down. This makes humans indispensable, because only humans have this ability: entering an environment and acquiring such context. If this problem were solved, I think certain problems could be solved to a large extent. Most people in the world are not Steve Jobs or Einstein. They may be ordinary people whose mathematical reasoning ability, or whatever, is not stronger than o3's, but they can manage context. After someone has been at a company for seven days, beyond what they have read in text, they have accumulated context in their mind. That context gives you an advantage over o3. o3 does not have that context; you do. Although you are not as smart as o3, you have the context, so you perform better than o3.

items.question: How do you understand endogenous reward?
items.object: Endogenous reward
items.answer: As I just said, many innovators can do many things without external incentives because they have their own internal values or incentives. AI and neuroscience have actually studied this for a very long time. In some sense, babies have a curiosity-based or self-based reward. You see many babies play with toys, bite things with their mouths, or do other things. What reward have they gained? They have not received a promotion or pay raise; they have not gotten money or other external incentives. They are simply curious. They ask: if I do this, what will it feel like? If the feeling is new, then I can learn. That is it.

items.question: What do you see as the challenge in constructing intrinsic incentives for AI operating through language and reasoning?
items.object: Intrinsic incentives for AI operating through language and reasoning
items.answer: Curiosity, a sense of control, or a sense of security—there are such intrinsic motivations that make infants do these things. Otherwise, it is hard to explain rationally why they would do them. But interestingly, when you are an infant, your understanding of the world is based on vision, physics, and the physical world. You learn how to combine touch, hearing, vision, and all the abilities involved in using your skeleton. But when you grow up, you have a language-, reasoning-, or text-based understanding of the world: how the world works; how I can start a company; get promoted; do all kinds of things. You are no longer playing a physical game; you are playing a language game. In that language game, there are of course intrinsic incentives too, but they seem quite different. I think that is today's challenge. In traditional AI, if you play a maze or a robot simulation, it can define intrinsic incentives based on world models or various motivations humans have as infants. But when you are playing a language game, how do you construct intrinsic incentives? That seems very different.

items.question: How has your view of learning from human intelligence in AI research evolved?
items.object: Learning from human intelligence when designing AI systems
items.answer: My biggest realization is that humans can generalize because they can reason. I think that may be the most important takeaway. This is interesting because in 2018, at MIT, I was in Josh Tenenbaum's lab—he is a major figure in cognitive science—and I learned a lot of cognitive science. The central story in cognitive science or computational cognitive science is: although today's AI has made much progress, it has many problems. We should look at what advantages humans have, how humans do these things, and why humans can do them better. For example, humans can generalize from a few samples while machines cannot. Why? We should seek methods from humans and apply them to AI. Later, though, I came to think that AI systems that work today are still very different from humans. Scaling laws, RL, and many things are very different from how humans learn. A better way to learn from humans may be to ask what humans can do that machines currently cannot. That is an objective fact. Once you identify the problem, you can reason from first principles about how to solve it; you do not necessarily have to rely on how humans solve it. For example, I can join a company, work for seven days or intern for three months, accumulate the company context, and—although I may not be especially smart, perhaps a graduate of a second-tier or first-tier university—I can do many things AI cannot currently do. That is an objective fact. How do we solve it? Cognitive science or neuroscience may tell you that the human brain has a hippocampus, episodic memory, or some such architecture. But you may not need to copy that completely; you can design long-term memory from first principles. What can robustly and objectively be learned from humans is what people can do that machines cannot. How humans do it, and how much we should borrow from their methods, is more subjective and nuanced. Neuroscience and cognitive science have not solved these problems completely; they only offer hypotheses. And even if something is confirmed—for example, human vision is relatively more deeply and thoroughly studied; humans have a six-layer cortex, with different structures in each layer—the takeaway can be that I need a neural network, but I do not need to copy every detail.

items.question: How do you decide whether an AI agent should become more human-like?
items.object: Human-like behavior in agent design
items.answer: I think it is a utility problem. For many problems, being unlike humans is more valuable—for example, playing Go or, I do not know, driving. Most people may not drive very well, right? There may be a better way to drive based on rules. But for things where being human-like is better, you should think about how to bridge the gap. For Go or games, through RL I can learn a way that differs from humans and is better than humans, so I should not imitate humans. But in working at a company, getting along well with your boss, and completing all kinds of tasks, humans currently do this better than AI. Then we should try to become more human-like.

items.answer: I think that is possible. Ultimately, these things will still arise from utility. If something has value, it may emerge. For example, many people may be lonely and need a friend. In that case you will not anthropomorphize it. So I think it will still be based on the economic value of the thing.

items.question: How do you think about whether AI will lead to greater centralization or decentralization in society?
items.object: AI, centralization, and individual opportunity
items.answer:
I think a core question may be whether this technology evolves toward greater centralization or decentralization. There are arguments on both sides. The centralization argument is that new super-companies such as OpenAI or Anthropic could become one-trillion-, ten-trillion-, or hundred-trillion-dollar companies; they could control most resources and compute, create a super app or super platform, and have enormous centralized advantages. The decentralization argument is that each individual can be empowered. The reason there are large differences between people today includes information gaps, cognitive gaps, and intelligence gaps. If intelligence becomes very cheap, like electricity, then it can empower most people to some extent. I find this interesting.

My recent thinking is that human society is a network. It has two important properties. One is its degree of centralization, or the concentration of resource allocation. Primitive society may have been very egalitarian, but as technology developed it became increasingly centralized—the Pareto principle, the Matthew effect, whatever. The other dimension is the probability or speed with which you can succeed in entrepreneurship or move from the edge of the network to its center. To some extent, over the past few centuries, the network has become more centralized: wealth inequality has grown, or there is the Pareto principle and the Matthew effect. But at the same time, poor people or ordinary people may have more opportunities. In ancient times—under clan systems, the Nine-Rank System, European aristocracy, or India's caste system—farmers might remain farmers forever; there was class rigidity. The apparent trend of technological development is that both intensify: centralization intensifies because of efficiency, which is a fundamental reason, while opportunities to create new things, at least so far, have also increased. But it is hard to say what the future social trend will be. It may continue, but it may not.

items.question: How do you understand OpenAI's decision to make GPT its distinctive bet after initially focusing on reinforcement learning?
items.object: OpenAI's shift from reinforcement learning to GPT
items.answer: This is my own summary and speculation. I think OpenAI is a very bottom-up company. Its first seven or eight years were like a research lab, with all kinds of ideas and attempts; different people probably had different ideas. Objectively, at the start it focused on reinforcement learning, because that was the hottest thing then. When DeepMind was founded around 2015, the hottest AI company was DeepMind, and its most successful work was reinforcement learning. Before GPT, AlphaGo was perhaps the most successful AI project. So naturally you would work on RL. But to surpass the previous dominant player, you need a different bet. If OpenAI had kept doing RL, it would probably have been hard to surpass DeepMind. Even if you did it well, or did some tasks better than DeepMind, people would still think of DeepMind when they thought of RL. GPT turned out to be that different bet. Of course, it was highly non-consensus at the time. I can tell a story: my advisor was the second author of GPT-1. He stayed at OpenAI for a year and then became a professor at Princeton. At the time he was somewhat skeptical, because the results were not especially good—the leaderboard scores were not the highest—and you used many GPUs to do this. There were also scaling laws that had just emerged in 2017, and Ilya told my advisor, 'Carl, look, this prophecy has already been solved by us. Now we just need to scale up, and this thing is over.' But even at OpenAI, even in that environment, even as a GPT author, there may still not have been consensus. So I think they did something very contrarian at the time. Now it is consensus; you need to look for the next contrarian thing, perhaps.

items.question: How do you understand the role of reinforcement learning in OpenAI’s research strategy as GPT became a major focus?
items.object: Reinforcement learning and OpenAI’s allocation of research resources
items.answer: I think reinforcement learning was always important. Even when I was working on GPT, Jiang Shuman and others were still—there were still people working on RL. It was not that after doing GPT we threw all RL away. It was more that perhaps 70% or 80% of company resources went into this, while some other things continued. This was important because ChatGPT's success later proved that RL was also very important. Without RLHF and alignment techniques, it could not have become a product. History was not: I took one path, completely abandoned it, took another path, and then returned to the first. It was softer: I did many things; this one looked very promising, so I placed a larger bet on it, while continuing to work on some others.

items.question: Why do you see language as a uniquely powerful tool for generalization?
items.object: Language as a tool for generalization
items.answer: In some sense, language is also a tool invented by humans, like fire or a pen. But it is special because it is a generalizable tool that helps you solve any kind of problem. Once you learn it, you can do many new tasks. For example, you learn rock climbing, but it may not help you do many new tasks. Once you learn language, it almost always helps you do new tasks, because you can communicate with people, learn, think, and reason. To some extent, twenty years ago many people had not thought this through. They thought we have speech, text, images, video—these are all just data, so perhaps there is not much difference. But I think the biggest difference is that language is a tool humans invented to achieve generalization, and that is more fundamental than other things.

items.question: How do you understand the claim that reinforcement learning is gaining the ability to generalize?
items.object: Generalization in reinforcement learning
items.answer: I would call it a personal view, though many people are discussing it. Whether something generalizes is of course a spectrum; it is relative, not an absolute zero-or-one matter. I say this because previously, if you trained in one environment, you could only operate in that environment. Now, if you train in one environment, you can operate in more environments. I think that is the most essential difference. With DeepSeek, an interesting reported result is that you do RL on math and coding, but become stronger at creative writing too. That is an essential difference. AlphaGo can only play Go; it cannot play chess. But now, for example, if you learn mathematics, you can do creative writing. That is an essential difference.

items.question: How do you see the possibility of reinforcement learning producing a single model that can perform all tasks?
items.object: Cross-task generalization and the possibility of a single model that can perform all tasks
items.answer: It is hard to say. Even reasoning may generalize differently across different environments. Logic-based reasoning may transfer more readily from mathematics to coding, while reasoning based on social dynamics may transfer better to other tasks. But I think the important thing is that we may now finally have a possible single model that can do all tasks. Previously we thought that was unlikely; now I think it may be possible. You can do RL across many different tasks, and it can transfer to more tasks. But if you only consider transfer between tasks, the degree of transfer is certainly related to the nature of the tasks.

items.question: How do you think AI agents should scale when their compute costs are so high?
items.object: Scaling AI agents by finding valuable applications
items.answer: I think the most important point may be to find a good application. Cost itself is not the problem; the problem is when your cost does not justify your performance or value. If something has a lot of value, I spend $500 and it earns me $1,000—that is not a problem. At present, the most important thing is to find a valuable application. Costs will always come down: model capabilities will improve, and prices and costs will fall. But finding a good, valuable application is fundamental. Different applications call for different approaches. For a simple task, I can train a small model that is faster, cheaper, and more specific to that task. For something harder, such as investing or deep research, I may need a large model, and use different methods to balance cost and value. But first find something valuable; once you have found it, there will always be ways to reduce the cost.

items.question: How do you think a research background affects someone's prospects as an AI agent founder?
items.object: Research backgrounds among AI agent founders
items.answer: It is hard to say; I think it depends a lot on the person. It is hard to divide people into researchers and non-researchers and say those categories differ strongly. People differ greatly from one another. The most important thing is still to find value. Call it product-market fit, product sense, or whatever—you need to find that value. Technology is only a means for now. The key is solving problems and finding good problems. In fact, a strong research, NLP, or related background may be a disadvantage because you become too attached to the technology and use a hammer to look for nails. Looking at it now, the founders of the most successful applications do not seem to be people doing NLP or AI. Cursor was four undergraduates. Of course, Professor's founder seems to be a researcher. items.question: How do you understand the relationship between AI startups and large model companies when it comes to copying product innovations?
items.object: Mutual copying between AI startups and large model companies
items.answer: Let me say a little more based on Midas. Traditionally, people think a large company builds something first, and then startups can copy it. For example, I build ChatGPT, and others can copy ChatGPT or make something similar. But now it seems the reverse can also work: a small company can make something first, creating an interaction or product innovation, and model companies can learn from or apply it. I find that interesting. People often say that models keep improving and are just making a wedding dress for startups, because you create a great model but if you do not apply it especially well yourself, startups will. But conversely, if you create an excellent interaction mode but cannot make its model or underlying capabilities especially strong, large companies can learn that interaction mode, add their model capabilities, and do it very well too. So perhaps the world is one of mutual copying, rather than one-way copying. That is my personal view.

items.question: How has DeepSeek prompted you to reconsider open-source AI models?
items.object: DeepSeek's challenge to assumptions about open-source AI models
items.answer: Another point is reconsidering open source. Sam also said much about this on Twitter: OpenAI overlooked it, but upon reflection it has value and perhaps should be done. We tend to assume open source will lag far behind closed source, because building these models is not like Linux or operating systems, where a thousand people can each contribute something and make it good through distributed properties. Building a model seems more like having twenty exceptional people and a great deal of money; you need a very special organization, highly concentrated resources, and very special people. In that situation, traditional open-source advantages are not large. And Facebook's open-source work may not have been so good, so people in the United States may have habitually overlooked this. Doing open source well is non-trivial: you need sufficient resources, strong people, good organizational culture, and business justification. The best case is that you are a philanthropist with tens of billions and do it to benefit the world. That is a low-probability event, but it happened: someone like that did it. It is worth reflecting on. I also think DeepSeek has many admirable aspects, including its organizational structure, engineering, and infrastructure.

items.question: How do you envision the future agent ecosystem?

items.question: How do you understand the environment's role in the memory hierarchy of agents and people?

For example, I plug in or remove a USB drive, upload something to the internet, or make music and turn it into a CD. The external world is always the outermost layer of the memory hierarchy. The winter before last, I read the final book von Neumann wrote before he died, called The Brain and the Computer. items.question: Why do you see the current moment in AI as an inflection point that warrants calling your article “Second Half”?
items.object: The methodological inflection point behind the title “Second Half”
items.answer: Because, methodologically, I think we have just reached something like an inflection-point moment: we finally have a very general method that can solve all kinds of problems. If you asked an AI researcher ten years ago, they would have thought that doing translation, playing games, using a computer to book tickets, and doing mathematics were completely different things. They required entirely different methods, entirely different people with different knowledge, and completely different communities, right? They attended entirely different conferences and had entirely different papers; these things were unrelated. But now, these things can finally all be solved with one method. This is a fundamentally inflection-point event at the methodological level.

items.question: How do you understand pre-training’s role in making reinforcement learning and agents possible?
items.object: Pre-training as a foundation for language-based reinforcement learning and agents
items.answer: Agents are what we want to achieve, right? Pre-training and RL are both parts of the technology needed to achieve that. But of course, you could also say pre-training laid the groundwork for RL, because without pre-training it is very hard to do RL in these text-based environments. I think that is highly non-trivial, because traditionally RL people do not care about priors; they do not care about pre-training or prior knowledge. They think: I have an environment and I have a reward; it's a matter of time, it's a matter of samples that I can solve the environment. In other words, I can theoretically prove that even with something like the internet, even without pre-training, as long as I have enough samples, I can still solve the problem by brute force—as long as you define the reward well enough and my training and test rewards come from the same distribution. But the number of samples may mean it needs to learn for, say, 10 to the 34th years. It may never learn, in the sense of the age of the universe. From that perspective, pre-training laid the foundation for language-based RL. In theory you could still do it without that, but in practice you cannot.

items.question: How do you judge whether it makes sense for technology companies to invest in pre-training again?

items.answer: I think there is a tradeoff between cost and value. items.question: How do you think an agent’s application should shape the choice between pre-training and reinforcement learning?
items.object: Choosing between pre-training and reinforcement learning for different agent applications
items.answer: One immature thought of mine is that different applications may require different forms of agents, and they may be constructed differently. For example, suppose all I need is to play Go; then I can simply build AlphaGo. I do not need pre-training or anything else. If I have a very vertical domain where the value is large enough, I have lots of data, and I can trust the closed loop, then perhaps something mainly based on RL can work. At some level, systems like Google Ads or TikTok recommendations are a bit like this. I find a sufficiently closed environment and do something RL-like, and it can create enough value. That is reasonable. But many long-tail things in the world require generalization. They require building something human-like: even if you do not know everything, you can learn; you can learn online, enter a new company, adapt to its environment, and do new things. In that case, pre-training may be more important because you need more generalization. So I think different applications may have different technical paths. But technical paths are tools. As long as your value exceeds your cost, the choice of technology is flexible. There is no one technical path that must win. As long as it makes economic sense, it is possible.

items.question: How would you approach AI strategy as the CEO of a large global technology company with no model of its own, no strong research culture, and no good AI strategy?
items.object: AI strategy for a large technology company without its own model or strong research culture
items.answer: First, I would definitely learn. I would want to learn what this thing actually is. If, as CEO, you do not understand it, then everything is difficult. Often a company’s bottleneck is the CEO’s level of understanding of the matter. If you do not understand it and say, “I’ll hire some very good people and do some things,” then they may fool you, right? So first, you need to learn it yourself. Then I think you should still think from the perspective of creating new value. After all, you are not a technical expert; you are the CEO of a company, and you have certain scenarios, resources, and advantages. From first principles, a new technology has emerged, and what you need to think about is how to use that technology together with your current resources to create new value. Of course, you can try to make something completely different from what exists now, with very great value, like ChatGPT. But for most companies, even very wealthy and capable ones, that may not make sense. First learn the technology yourself; second, think about what new value you can create.

items.question: How do you understand the disagreement over whether AI companies’ safety responsibilities should extend beyond their products?
items.object: Product safety versus broader AI safety responsibilities
items.answer: I think safety is a very complex issue. When everyone says “safety,” they may actually have different things in mind. My view is this: I think the main current disagreement is whether it is enough to treat safety seriously in the normal way a commercial company does, or whether you need a broader safety responsibility. For example, for ChatGPT, if it is unsafe and deletes your things, then the product has failed and has no commercial value. So even for commercial value, it will take many safety issues seriously. Every product is like that: based on its product and business, it will naturally value safety, because if something is unsafe, it is simply not a good product. People will not use it, and it has no value. But I think the main disagreement now is whether you need safety beyond the product itself, or something more ideological. This has not yet been fully defined clearly. The former is easy to solve, I think. If you have a good application, you will always find ways to solve safety problems, I believe. Once something has enough value, someone will need to solve the safety problem, because solving it is a necessary condition for realizing that value. As long as the value is large enough, it will always be solved. As for the latter, I think there is a great deal of uncertainty. It is hard for me to assess.

items.answer: I think consciousness is something that has not been well defined. items.question: What do you think made your approach to AI research during your PhD fruitful?
items.object: Research priorities behind his PhD work in AI
items.answer: There are two lines in what I wanted to do. One is simple, general methods; the other is different tasks with real practical value, where those tasks are often about how to create new value in the real digital world. Traditional tasks either create tasks in a fake digital world, such as games or exams, or create value in the physical world. But I think the real digital world—computers, coding, or the web—is virgin territory, an enormous treasure trove. I happened to excavate some of it. Then the emergence of GPT-3, of these models, and of reasoning created an opportunity to develop some simple, general methods. There were also factors of timing. There happened to be such opportunities, and these were, I think, the most important things for AI: on one hand, simple general methods; on the other, better task environments. I think you need to think boldly enough and generally enough. If you work on a task with a very low ceiling, then what does it matter even if you solve it? You need to take on tasks that, even now, seem very hard.

items.question: Why do you see finding a fit between a research method and a task as the hardest part of your research?
items.object: Method-task fit in research
items.answer:
I think my experience may be unusual, because most good methods are proposed because there is a particular task, and that particular task happens to inspire a very general method. For example, PPO may initially have been for a specific thing, or Transformer may initially have been for a specific thing. I think a class of work on attention was deeply influenced by translation. If you happened to be working on translation at that point in time, you were very likely to make something great. At that time, the task best suited to studying attention mechanisms was something like translation, because you naturally need to attend to different parts of a sequence, and that attention may not be linear; you need a method like Transformer. Most of the time, people discover great methods because they have a task they need to solve, and it happens to be general enough.

But I think my experience is unusual because often I first think of something in my head that I believe is very general and good, and then I need to find tasks to prove that it is general, good, or will be valuable in the future. It may not have enough value yet, but you need to find simple tasks now to demonstrate its value. I think that is very difficult. Just as entrepreneurship requires product-market fit, research requires method-task fit. That is the hardest part.

items.question: How do you think about the most ambitious tasks you could set for AI?
items.object: Ambitious tasks for AI in science and economic organization
items.answer: I think in this era, however radical something is, it may no longer be called radical. I think anything is possible. Before I graduated, what I thought about more was how to create an Einstein, or how to create a scientist. At that time I was still more of an academia person—more in the academic world, right? At Princeton, naturally your idols are von Neumann and Einstein. So naturally, the most interesting task you can think of is: can I discover the next theory of relativity? Can I discover the next great scientific theory? I think that would undoubtedly signal that AGI or ASI had been achieved—AI discovers a theory of everything. After coming to Silicon Valley, to California, and into companies, I came to think that human organizations are also very interesting. If one could create a new company—a company with a one-trillion-dollar GBA—I think that would be very interesting. Creating economic value is also difficult; it is difficult in a different way from inventing relativity.

items.question: How do you understand the role of natural language as a general representation for humans and AI?
items.object: Natural language as a general representation for humans and AI
items.answer: I think in a particular domain there will certainly be representations better than language. For example, in Go, thinking in natural language may not be the optimal method. But language did not arise for efficiency in handling a particular task, or for communication about one particular task. It arose to connect all tasks, or connect human cognitive capabilities, and form a general representation. So it was not optimized to be best for a particular task. You will often find that it has much redundancy in a particular task, but overall it is general. And of course, just as we can create a new language, AI can certainly create a new language. It might be more efficient or something. But I think English, or something based on English, will probably still become a mainstream language in the end, because humans already have such strong priors and prior knowledge. People also have a value orientation or motivation to make machine language more like humans, so that we can better understand it, control it, monitor it, change it, and manipulate it. That seems like a natural choice.

items.question: How do you interpret your advisor’s advice that if someone else can do something, it is okay to let them do it?
items.object: His advisor’s advice to let others pursue work they can do
items.answer: The thing my advisor said that influenced or impressed me most deeply was this. We would discuss a common situation in academia: you have an idea, and someone else does it, and then you are frustrated. He would say, “If someone else can do it, then it's okay to let them do it.” If you look at it from the perspective of humanity as a whole, if many people can do something, then perhaps it makes no difference if someone else does it. It seems to make no difference to society or the whole. Of course, I remember mentioning this, and someone said it was very fake, because in the end you find that nothing in this world is irreplaceable. Even if relativity had not been proposed, someone would have proposed it. There is nothing such that if you die or are absent, someone else cannot propose it. But I still think the statement makes sense. If you can clearly see that others are doing this thing, or something similar, you can choose to compete with them. If you do, perhaps you believe you will be more efficient or can do it better; I think that is reasonable too. Or you can explore something different. Ultimately, you need to create value for society. And one fortunate thing about this era is that this technology is very general and very great, and there is enough room to explore. Coding is an obviously popular thing that everyone is doing. Perhaps my value was to show the earliest initial signal; if others can do it, I think it is okay for them to do it as well.
